extracted.intended_audience: employers, immigration attorneys, stakeholders, and policymakers involved in H-1B petitions and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for designing and evaluating USCIS's H-1B cap-selection process, especially the proposed wage-level weighted, beneficiary-centric registration and selection procedures. Includes legal justification, empirical support, and responses to public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory gap-filling authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute does not expressly refer to allocation by random selection or address how numerical allocations should be administered when demand exceeds the available supply of H-1B visa numbers; DHS may permissibly fill that silence and implement reasonable selection procedures under its general statutory authority (e.g., INA secs. 103(a), 214(a), and (c)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS relies on reasoned decision making and precedent (e.g., Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo; Liu v. Mayorkas; Walker Macy). The agency may prescribe rules to fill statutory gaps and is not constrained to the single method of random selection merely because prior regulations used it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with program purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection methods should be consistent with the overarching statutory and programmatic goals: selecting highly skilled and highly paid nonimmigrants while protecting the wages, working conditions, and job opportunities of U.S. workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating selection procedures, consider whether the approach furthers Congress’s aim for the H-1B classification (e.g., helping U.S. employers fill labor shortages in positions requiring highly skilled workers) and whether it safeguards domestic labor market interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage-level-based weighted selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement a selection process that prioritizes selection generally based on the highest prevailing wage level that a proffered wage equals or exceeds (i.e., a wage-based weighting of registrations for unique beneficiaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion supports favoring higher-skilled/higher-paid beneficiaries in years of excess demand. DHS describes this as a reasonable method of filling the statutory silence about allocation methodology and as consistent with the program’s goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain access for all wage levels
rubrics_metrics.description: A weighted, wage-based selection process must not effectively preclude selection opportunities for beneficiaries at lower wage levels; employers should retain the opportunity to secure H-1B workers at all wage levels and in all eligible occupations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though weighted toward higher wage levels, the rule should preserve selection chances across wage levels and guard against total exclusion of lower-wage beneficiaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary as proxy for skill and value
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS views salary (the proffered wage relative to OEWS prevailing wage levels) as generally a reasonable proxy for skill level, experience, or the beneficiary’s value to the employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS cites data (e.g., FY2019–FY2024 median wages by wage level in certain occupations) to support a correlation between higher wages and higher skill/wage levels, while acknowledging some exceptions and employer-driven wage-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beneficiary-centric selection and anti-gaming
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection process should be beneficiary-centric (selecting unique beneficiaries rather than registrations) to prevent gaming—such as multiple registrations for the same beneficiary by cooperating entities—to unfairly increase selection odds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Builds on the 2024 beneficiary-centric final rule: selection remains beneficiary-centric but introduces wage-based weighting of unique beneficiaries. Anti-gaming rationale: reduces the ability of actors to inflate an individual’s selection probability via multiple registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness over pure randomization
rubrics_metrics.description: While random selection has been implemented and is reasonable, pure randomization is neither the only nor necessarily the optimal method when it does not serve the ends of the H-1B program or congressional intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether randomization best advances program goals (e.g., prioritizing high-skill labor and protecting U.S. workers). DHS argues that a weighted approach better serves these ends in years of excess demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical support and data-driven justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to selection procedures should be justified with empirical data (for example, DHS cites FY2019–FY2024 filings showing underrepresentation of wage level III and IV beneficiaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use program data (e.g., OPQ, CLAIMS3, ELIS, LCA disclosures) and other studies to demonstrate correlations and program effects that motivate the selection approach. DHS uses such data to show wage-level representation and to support the wage-as-proxy rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with prior rulemakings and court decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule should address prior related rulemakings and relevant court decisions (e.g., Chamber of Commerce v. DHS; Walker Macy; Liu) and explain why the current approach avoids the legal defects of prior efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide legal analysis showing how the final rule is a permissible exercise of statutory authority and how it aligns with or distinguishes controlling and persuasive precedent; anticipate and respond to predictable legal challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and specificity of definitions and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule should clearly define key terms and specify how aspects will be measured or treated—e.g., how 'wage' will be computed for remote work and split worksites, how part-time versus full-time work is treated, how wage amendments after approval are handled, and how wage levels will be set or updated—and describe enforcement mechanisms to prevent wage manipulation or post-selection abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address commenters’ requests for specificity by including precise definitions, computational rules, update mechanisms, and enforcement/anti-fraud provisions to prevent manipulation of wages, post-selection wage reductions, or misreporting of worksites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational comparability and non‑occupation prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying prevailing wage levels across occupations, account for the fact that OEWS wage levels are constructed to compare within occupations (and by geography) and not necessarily across occupations; the selection approach should not inadvertently prioritize certain occupations over others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize examples where high-skill occupations may receive lower wage-level classifications and design weighting to avoid unfair cross‑occupation distortions; DHS asserts the rule is not intended to prioritize particular occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative priority and handling of simultaneous submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier-filed registrations and petitions receive priority over later ones; if an insufficient number of registrations are received during the initial registration period, registration remains open and selection continues on a rolling basis until enough unique beneficiary registrations meet the cap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow regulatory provisions (e.g., 8 CFR 214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)(i)) and past practice (e.g., continued rolling selection after initial period if insufficient registrations) to ensure efficient administration and fair ordering among simultaneous submissions.
